12.Option: The timing of the excess mortality in 2022–2023 coincided with the peak of the Covid-19 vaccine rollout, suggesting that the vaccines may have contributed to increased mortality.
Evidence: Aotearoa New Zealand used a combination of border and community control measures to minimize transmission of SARS-CoV-2 until high vaccine coverage was achieved in late 2021 [ 2 , 3 ].
Following the establishment of the B.1.1.529 (Omicron) variant in January 2022 [ 4 ], New Zealand experienced a series of Covid-19 waves [ 5 ].

Covid-19-attributed deaths were extremely low in 2020 and 2021 (26 in each year). In 2022–23, the number of Covid-19-attributed deaths was close to the central estimate for excess deaths ( Fig. 3a , blue), accounting for 102% of the estimated excess in 2022 and 82% in 2023, and fell within the 95% CI in both years.
Covid-19 deaths and excess deaths, according to the quasi-Poisson regression model, followed similar trends in 2022–23.
12.Rationale: The passage makes no claim linking vaccine rollout to increased mortality. It states high vaccine coverage was achieved in late 2021 and that the excess mortality in 2022–23 closely matched Covid-19-attributed deaths and trends, implying Covid-19 infection (including Omicron waves) explained the excess. There is no evidence in the passage that vaccines caused increased mortality; on the contrary, timing described attributes excess to Covid-19 waves rather than vaccination.

12.Option: The bulk of the excess mortality observed in New Zealand during 2022–23 was directly attributable to Covid-19, either as an underlying or contributory cause of death.
Evidence: In 2022–23, the number of Covid-19-attributed deaths was close to the central estimate for excess deaths ( Fig. 3a , blue), accounting for 102% of the estimated excess in 2022 and 82% in 2023, and fell within the 95% CI in both years.
Covid-19 deaths and excess deaths, according to the quasi-Poisson regression model, followed similar trends in 2022–23.

The number of Covid-19 deaths fell within the 95% CI for the number of excess deaths in each age band (0–59 years, 60–69 years, 70–79 years, and 80+ years) and for both sexes in 2022 and 2023 ( Fig. 4 ).
12.Rationale: The passage provides direct quantitative evidence that Covid-19-attributed deaths accounted for essentially all of the estimated excess mortality in 2022 and the majority in 2023 (102% and 82% respectively), with Covid-19 death counts tracking the excess-death trends and falling within uncertainty bounds across age bands and sexes. These statements support the inference that most of the excess mortality in 2022–23 was directly attributable to Covid-19.

14.Option: The exclusion of individuals with diabetes in earlier observational analyses may have led to an underestimation of the true effect of BMI on mortality due to the removal of a key confounding factor.
Evidence: Participants with diabetes were therefore excluded from the observational analyses of adiposity and mortality, but this exclusion may have resulted in underestimation of the full effect of adiposity on mortality by removing, at least in part, the impact of adiposity on mortality that is mediated through diabetes.

Excess adiposity causes diabetes, but persistent hyperglycaemia in diabetes can itself cause pathological weight loss, distorting the observed associations of adiposity with prevalent diabetes and with cause-specific mortality [3].
14.Rationale: The passage does state that excluding participants with diabetes from earlier observational analyses may have led to underestimation of the full effect of adiposity on mortality. However, the option characterizes diabetes as a "key confounding factor." The passage describes diabetes primarily as a mediator (adiposity causes diabetes, and diabetes then contributes to mortality) and as a source of reverse causality (hyperglycaemia causing weight loss), not as a confounder. Thus the core claim of underestimation is supported, but the mechanistic wording in the option (removal of a confounding factor) contradicts the passage's framing (removal of a mediated effect/reverse-causality issue). Because the option misstates the causal role of diabetes, it is not derivable as written from the passage.

14.Option: The use of a trans-ancestry BMI genetic score in the current study may have introduced bias due to differences in allele frequencies across ancestral groups, leading to an overestimation of the effect of BMI on mortality.
Evidence: The BMI-GS created from the trans-ancestry meta-analysis comprised 724 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs).
In both men and women, these slopes were slightly shallower in older participants and in those with the highest proportion of Indigenous American ancestry.

Sensitivity analyses in which a less stringent clumping threshold was used, or in which those with diabetes or other chronic disease were excluded from the estimated association of the BMI-GS with BMI, or that were based on a BMI-GS derived from the GIANT consortium genome wide association study (GWAS) gave broadly similar estimates (Supplementary Figures S3–S5, though the HRs when using the GIANT consortium GWAS were a little higher).
14.Rationale: The passage documents use of a trans-ancestry BMI genetic score and notes small differences in the BMI-GS-to-BMI slopes by age and ancestry. However, it provides no direct evidence that the trans-ancestry score introduced bias that overestimated BMI effects on mortality. On the contrary, sensitivity analyses (including use of a GWAS-derived BMI-GS from another consortium) produced broadly similar estimates, arguing against a large bias from the instrument. The specific causal assertion in the option (bias due to allele frequency differences leading to overestimation) is not supported by text in the passage and therefore cannot be derived from it.

14.Option: The longer follow-up period in the current study compared to earlier analyses may have allowed for the detection of more pronounced associations between BMI and mortality.
Evidence: Previous analyses of the Mexico City Prospective Study (MCPS)—a cohort of 150,000 Mexican adults recruited 20 years ago—found that hyperglycaemia in diabetes was common and associated with a quadrupling in all-cause mortality at ages 35–74 years [4].
During a median of 20 years of follow-up, a total of 13,066 deaths occurred at ages 35–74 years...
14.Rationale: The passage states the cohort was recruited 20 years ago and that the current analyses have a median of 20 years of follow-up, but it does not present a comparison of follow-up durations between earlier analyses and the current study nor claim that increased follow-up explains differences in associations. The passage attributes differences to issues such as reverse causality, exclusion of diabetics in earlier observational analyses, and the use of MR to estimate lifelong effects. Therefore, the claim that longer follow-up is the explanatory factor is not supported by text in the passage.

14.Option: The magnitude of the associations reported in the current analysis of this Mexican population is somewhat greater than reported in previous MR studies conducted in European ancestry populations, suggesting that genetic effects on BMI are stronger in admixed populations.
Evidence: Previous MR studies conducted mostly in populations of European ancestry support the causal relevance of adiposity to cardiometabolic diseases and all-cause mortality [7–9] and have identified individual diseases most strongly associated with adiposity [10,11].

Evidence from non-European populations with admixed ancestry remains scarce. To address this gap, we used MR approaches to estimate the causal relevance of lifelong differences in BMI for cause-specific mortality among 125,000 Mexican adults with admixed ancestry previously enrolled into the MCPS [12].

Sensitivity analyses... that were based on a BMI-GS derived from the GIANT consortium genome wide association study (GWAS) gave broadly similar estimates (Supplementary Figures S3–S5, though the HRs when using the GIANT consortium GWAS were a little higher).
14.Rationale: While the passage notes that most prior MR studies have been in European ancestry populations and that non-European evidence is scarce, it does not state that the current MR effect sizes are larger than those in European studies or that genetic effects on BMI are inherently stronger in admixed populations. The passage provides no direct comparative quantitative evidence to support the option's claim. Thus the conclusion about stronger genetic effects in admixed populations cannot be drawn from the passage.

14.Option: The larger relative risks of all-cause mortality associated with higher genetically predicted BMI in the current report may be explained by the inclusion of the lifelong effects of BMI on mortality that are mediated through diabetes, which were not fully captured in previous observational analyses.
Evidence: Mendelian randomization (MR) approaches can mitigate biases due to reverse causality and confounding that are inherent in observational studies and seek to estimate the effects of lifelong differences in exposures on disease risks [6].

Participants with diabetes were therefore excluded from the observational analyses of adiposity and mortality, but this exclusion may have resulted in underestimation of the full effect of adiposity on mortality by removing, at least in part, the impact of adiposity on mortality that is mediated through diabetes.

Adjustment for genetic diabetes liability reduced the magnitude of the all-cause mortality log HR associated with the genetically predicted BMI by more than half [from ln(1.68) to ln(1.25) for all-cause mortality—a 56% reduction in magnitude (95% CI 35% to 94%)].
14.Rationale: The passage explicitly states that MR estimates lifelong effects and that excluding participants with diabetes in prior observational analyses could remove the portion of adiposity's effect on mortality mediated via diabetes, leading to underestimation. The mediation analysis presented shows that a large fraction (about 56%) of the genetically predicted BMI effect on all-cause mortality is mediated through genetic diabetes liability. Together, these statements directly support the option that inclusion of lifelong BMI effects mediated through diabetes in the current MR-based analysis explains the larger relative risks observed compared with earlier observational analyses.

15.Option: Despite the growing prominence of the interventional framework in epidemiology, most studies that aimed to estimate intervention effects did not specify a 'how' that adhered to consistency, and only a minority of these studies had well-defined interventions.
Evidence: As the interventional framing and well-defined intervention assumption become more widely adopted, ‘causal effects’ and ‘intervention effects’ become synonyms [ 5 , 21–23 , 28 , 29 ].

We categorized 20% of studies (29/146, Table 2 ) as intervention-effect studies because they stated their exposure contrast in terms of a hypothetical intervention ( Supplementary Table S2 , available at IJE online, contains details).
Of the 29 intervention-effect studies, only one (3%) detailed how the exposure would be intervened upon ( Table 2 ).
Only 38% (11/29) of intervention-effect studies had well-defined interventions ( Table 2 ; interrater reliability: kappa = 0.85).
15.Rationale: The passage explicitly states that the interventional framing is increasingly adopted, that 29 studies were classified as intervention-effect studies, and that only 1/29 (3%) provided a detailed 'how'. It further reports only 38% of these intervention-effect studies had well-defined interventions. Together these statements directly support the inference that despite the framework's prominence, most intervention-effect studies did not specify a 'how' satisfying consistency and only a minority had well-defined interventions.

15.Option: Studies that failed to specify a 'how' for their intervention often implicitly assumed treatment variation irrelevance, but this assumption was rarely justified in the methods or discussion sections.
Evidence: Of the 29 intervention-effect studies, only one (3%) detailed how the exposure would be intervened upon ( Table 2 ).
The other 10 had well-defined interventions—without articulating a ‘how’ — because of treatment variation irrelevance.

In contrast, no intervention-effect studies of obesity/BMI, substance use, health behaviours, nutrition and/or physical activity had well-defined interventions ( Supplementary Table S3 , available at IJE online). In these studies, authors often described what their intervention was, but did not discuss why the various mechanisms through which the intervention could be achieved (i.e. the ‘hows’) would likely have similar effects on the outcome.

Thus, when studies of such exposures simply stated—without justification—that treatment variation irrelevance was assumed (or ignored the assumption entirely), we concluded they had ill-defined interventions.
15.Rationale: The passage shows that nearly all intervention-effect studies failed to specify a 'how' (only 1/29 did), and that some studies were judged to have well-defined interventions because authors invoked treatment variation irrelevance without articulating a 'how'. It also explicitly notes many subject-area studies did not discuss why different 'hows' would have similar effects and that, when authors assumed treatment variation irrelevance without justification, the reviewers judged interventions ill-defined. These statements support the inference that studies often relied on treatment variation irrelevance implicitly and that such assumptions were frequently unjustified in the manuscript.

15.Option: The lack of well-defined interventions in most studies is primarily due to the absence of detailed data on exposure mechanisms, particularly in observational studies of socio-structural factors.
Evidence: Moreover, epidemiological datasets often lack sufficient detail from which to operationalize well-defined interventions (e.g. datasets may contain information on respondents’ duration of physical activity but lack information on activity type). In such settings, satisfying the well-defined intervention assumption can be challenging.

In contrast, no intervention-effect studies of obesity/BMI, substance use, health behaviours, nutrition and/or physical activity had well-defined interventions ( Supplementary Table S3 , available at IJE online). In these studies, authors often described what their intervention was, but did not discuss why the various mechanisms through which the intervention could be achieved (i.e. the ‘hows’) would likely have similar effects on the outcome.
15.Rationale: The passage does note that epidemiological datasets can lack detail (e.g. activity type) and that this can make operationalizing well-defined interventions challenging, and it identifies certain subject areas (e.g. BMI, behavioural exposures) as lacking well-defined interventions. However, it does not assert that absence of detailed data on exposure mechanisms is the primary reason for the lack of well-defined interventions nor does it single out socio-structural factors as the main driver. The authors also emphasize failures to specify a 'how' and failures to justify treatment variation irrelevance as important reasons. Because the passage does not support the stronger causal claim that data absence is the primary cause (particularly for socio-structural factors), this option is not derivable from the passage.

15.Option: The interventional framework's emphasis on specifying a 'how' for interventions enhances the policy relevance of epidemiological findings by enabling predictions about real-world outcomes if the exposure contrast were applied.
Evidence: To satisfy the well-defined intervention assumption, textbooks and guidelines advocate conceptualizing exposures as treatments in hypothetical RCTs, even in observational settings [ 10 , 19 , 20 ]. Thus, when the well-defined intervention assumption is satisfied (along with other assumptions), causal effects can be interpreted as intervention effects: the effect an exposure would have on an outcome if it were modified by the hypothetical intervention [ 1 , 14 , 21 ].

This framing has several purported advantages. ... Third, it facilitates predicting the effects of actual interventions, making findings policy relevant [ 1 , 14 , 23 ]. For the latter two reasons, proponents encourage conceptualizing humanly feasible hypothetical interventions, although feasibility is not required [ 1 , 14 ].

According to textbooks and guidelines, specifying how an exposure would be intervened upon is key for estimating intervention effects, because different ‘hows’ can have different health effects [ 1 , 14 , 22 , 24 ]. Thus, failing to specify and operationalize the ‘how’ can cause consistency violations [ 1 , 14 , 22 ].
15.Rationale: The passage explicitly states that conceptualizing interventions and specifying the 'how' allow causal effects to be interpreted as intervention effects and that this framing facilitates predicting effects of actual interventions, making findings policy relevant. It also emphasizes that specifying 'how' is key because different 'hows' can yield different effects. Therefore, the inference that emphasizing a 'how' enhances policy relevance by enabling real-world predictions is directly supported by the text.

15.Option: The majority of studies using g-methods or TMLE failed to meet the consistency assumption because they did not define their exposure in terms of a hypothetical intervention, regardless of data quality.
Evidence: We categorized 20% of studies (29/146, Table 2 ) as intervention-effect studies because they stated their exposure contrast in terms of a hypothetical intervention ( Supplementary Table S2 , available at IJE online, contains details).
Of the 29 intervention-effect studies, only one (3%) detailed how the exposure would be intervened upon ( Table 2 ).
Of the three causal-inference assumptions, studies mentioned exchangeability most frequently (134/146, 92%); a minority mentioned consistency (62/146, 42%) or positivity (66/146, 45%) ( Table 2 ).
Only 38% (11/29) of intervention-effect studies had well-defined interventions ( Table 2 ; interrater reliability: kappa = 0.85).
15.Rationale: The passage does not state that a majority 'failed to meet the consistency assumption' because they did not define exposure as a hypothetical intervention. In fact, intervention-effect studies were explicitly those that stated their exposure contrast in terms of a hypothetical intervention (29 studies). The passage reports many studies did not detail the 'how' and that only 38% of intervention-effect studies had well-defined interventions, but it does not claim that the majority failed consistency solely due to not defining exposure as a hypothetical intervention. Additionally, the passage notes that a substantial fraction of studies mentioned the consistency assumption. The blanket causal statement 'failed to meet the consistency assumption... regardless of data quality' is stronger than the evidence presented and is not supported.

16.Option: The protective effects of increased BMI on tuberculosis risk are most pronounced among the most undernourished populations due to the nonlinear relationship between BMI and tuberculosis risk.
Evidence: The meta-analyses showed an inverse dose–response relationship between BMI and tuberculosis risk across all studied populations.

When fitting spline models, we found evidence for a nonlinear relationship with tuberculosis risk increasing faster at lower BMI values and decreasing more gradually at higher BMI values, particularly among people with HIV (e.g. coefficient for nonlinear term in the general population = 0.12, P < 0.001; Supplementary Table S3 and Figure 3 ).

In the piecewise linear models, the reduction in tuberculosis risk per one-unit increase in BMI was 18.0% (95% CI: 16.4–19.6) for BMI of <25.0 kg/m2 and 6.9% (95% CI: 4.6–9.2) for BMI of ≥25.0 kg/m2 in 22 general-population cohorts ( n = 24,921,531); 15.3% (95% CI: 13.1–17.5) for BMI of <23.0 kg/m2 and 2.6% (95% CI: –3.1–7.9) for BMI of ≥23.0 kg/m2 in 18 cohorts of people with HIV ( n = 162,609); and 20.5% (95% CI: 18.4–22.6) for BMI of <24.0 kg/m2 and 13.4% (95% CI: 3.9–22.0) for BMI of ≥24.0 kg/m2 in three cohorts of people with diabetes ( n = 1,118,424) ( Figure 3 ).
Using the spline model and assuming a mean BMI of 17.0 kg/m2 among underweight people globally versus a BMI of 25.6 kg/m2 among non-underweight people globally, the RR was 5.0 (95% CI: 4.2–5.9).
16.Rationale: The passage explicitly reports a nonlinear inverse relationship where tuberculosis risk increases faster at lower BMI values and quantifies much larger percent risk reductions per unit BMI increase at lower BMI ranges than at higher ranges (e.g. 18.0% per unit <25 vs 6.9% per unit ≥25 in general-population cohorts). The large RR (≈5.0) comparing mean BMIs typical of underweight vs non-underweight further indicates that the protective effect is most pronounced among the most undernourished. Therefore the inference follows directly from the presented data.

16.Option: The protective effect of higher BMI on tuberculosis risk is primarily due to reduced diabetes incidence, as higher BMI is associated with lower diabetes risk in populations with high tuberculosis burden.
Evidence: Undernutrition is the leading driver of tuberculosis, responsible for ∼10% of cases in 2023, which is higher than HIV, alcohol use disorders, smoking, and diabetes [ 2 , 5 ].

We classified studies by population (general population, people with HIV, and people with diabetes) and whether they were conducted in settings with a high tuberculosis burden or a lower tuberculosis burden, as defined by WHO [ 2 ]; we stratified our analyses by population and country tuberculosis burden (only possible for the general-population studies).
In the piecewise linear models, the reduction in tuberculosis risk per one-unit increase in BMI was ... 20.5% ... in three cohorts of people with diabetes ( n = 1,118,424) ( Figure 3 ).
16.Rationale: The passage provides no evidence that higher BMI protects against tuberculosis by reducing diabetes incidence. It states undernutrition (low BMI) is the leading driver of tuberculosis and separately analyzes cohorts of people with diabetes, but it does not assert or show that higher BMI lowers diabetes risk or that diabetes reduction mediates the BMI–tuberculosis relationship. In fact, diabetes is listed as one of multiple drivers of tuberculosis distinct from undernutrition. Thus the specific causal claim that the protective effect is primarily due to reduced diabetes incidence is not supported by the passage.

16.Option: Because the relationship between BMI and tuberculosis risk is nonlinear, the protective effect of nutritional improvement is equally strong across all BMI ranges, particularly in people with HIV and diabetes.
Evidence: When fitting spline models, we found evidence for a nonlinear relationship with tuberculosis risk increasing faster at lower BMI values and decreasing more gradually at higher BMI values, particularly among people with HIV (e.g. coefficient for nonlinear term in the general population = 0.12, P < 0.001; Supplementary Table S3 and Figure 3 ).

In the piecewise linear models, the reduction in tuberculosis risk per one-unit increase in BMI was 18.0% (95% CI: 16.4–19.6) for BMI of <25.0 kg/m2 and 6.9% (95% CI: 4.6–9.2) for BMI of ≥25.0 kg/m2 in 22 general-population cohorts ...; 15.3% (95% CI: 13.1–17.5) for BMI of <23.0 kg/m2 and 2.6% (95% CI: –3.1–7.9) for BMI of ≥23.0 kg/m2 in 18 cohorts of people with HIV ...; and 20.5% (95% CI: 18.4–22.6) for BMI of <24.0 kg/m2 and 13.4% (95% CI: 3.9–22.0) for BMI of ≥24.0 kg/m2 in three cohorts of people with diabetes ( n = 1,118,424) ( Figure 3 ).
16.Rationale: The passage demonstrates the relationship is nonlinear and explicitly reports that percent reductions in tuberculosis risk per unit BMI increase are substantially larger at lower BMI ranges than at higher ranges. Thus the protective effect is not equally strong across all BMI ranges; it is stronger at lower BMI values. The numeric results for people with HIV and diabetes also show disparities between BMI ranges, contradicting the claim of equal strength.

16.Option: The lack of evidence in settings with both high tuberculosis burden and high undernutrition means that the observed dose–response relationship cannot be generalized to low- and middle-income countries.
Evidence: There were also seven in the Region of the Americas ( n = 929,140; 3.5%) [ 27 – 33 ], 16 in the African Region ( n = 137,652; 0.53%) [ 34 – 48 ], and 4 in the South-East Asian region ( n = 24,051; 0.09%) [ 49 – 52 ].

There were important differences in populations, which ranged from general-population-based cohorts among healthy individuals (mostly in the Western Pacific Region) ... to specific cohorts of people with HIV (mostly in the African Region) ...
Similar values were obtained when including only studies performed in countries with a high tuberculosis burden or a lower tuberculosis burden ( Supplementary Figure S2 ).
The meta-analyses showed an inverse dose–response relationship between BMI and tuberculosis risk across all studied populations.
16.Rationale: The passage includes cohorts from multiple regions including the African Region and South-East Asia (areas with many LMICs) and specifically states that similar values were obtained when analyses were restricted to countries with high tuberculosis burden or lower burden. The meta-analyses found a consistent inverse dose–response relationship across studied populations. Therefore the statement that there is a lack of evidence for generalizing to LMICs is incorrect based on the data presented.

16.Option: The RATIONS trial demonstrated that nutritional support for household contacts of people with tuberculosis reduced the tuberculosis risk by ~40%, indicating that nutritional interventions are the most effective strategy for preventing tuberculosis in high-burden settings.
Evidence: After the removal of duplicates, our search yielded 8881 records, of which 127 articles were sought for full-text review. Forty studies describing 43 cohorts were included—34 (37 cohorts) identified in our new search and 6 from the 2009 review ( Figure 1 ). All were cohort studies (some embedded in randomized trials), with recruitment undertaken between 1949 and 2021.

The RR of tuberculosis associated with undernutrition in different population groups is shown in Table 2 . Using the spline model and assuming a mean BMI of 17.0 kg/m2 among underweight people globally versus a BMI of 25.6 kg/m2 among non-underweight people globally, the RR was 5.0 (95% CI: 4.2–5.9).
As this was a review of existing data and involved no primary data collection, ethical approvals were not required for this study.
16.Rationale: The passage does not mention a 'RATIONS' trial or report a ~40% reduction in tuberculosis risk from a nutritional intervention. It is a systematic review/meta-analysis of cohort data (some cohorts embedded in randomized trials), and it reports relative risks associated with undernutrition (e.g. RR ≈5.0 comparing mean underweight vs non-underweight BMIs). There is no evidence in the passage to support the specific trial result or the strong claim that nutritional interventions are the single most effective prevention strategy in high-burden settings. Therefore this option is not supported by the passage.

17.Option: Regions along international borders in Ethiopia, such as Afar, Benishangul-Gumuz, and Somali, are particularly lagging behind in achieving the WHO’s End TB target for TB incidence reduction, despite national progress.
Evidence: Conversely, the Afar, Somali, and Benishangul-Gumuz regions experienced an increase in incidence during the same period ( Fig. 1 ).

Regional estimates of progress toward achieving the WHO’s End TB targets revealed that all regions except Dire Dawa, Harari, and Sidama showed incidence reduction below the national average, which was estimated to be 31%.
These hot spots are primarily located in the north-eastern and south-eastern regions that are particularly prominent along the international borders with Eritrea and Djibouti.
This makes Ethiopia one of the seven high-TB-burden countries that achieved the WHO’s 2020 End TB Strategy milestone, with a 31.3% total reduction in incidence [ 15 ].
17.Rationale: The passage explicitly states that Afar, Somali, and Benishangul-Gumuz experienced increases in TB incidence between 2015 and 2020, and it reports that many regions had reductions below the national average (31%). Spatial analysis identifies hot spots of poor or increasing incidence clustered along international borders. Taken together, these statements support the inference that border regions (including Afar, Somali, and Benishangul-Gumuz) are lagging behind national progress toward the WHO End TB incidence reduction targets.

17.Option: Districts with better preparedness and resources for TB service are more likely to have high TB incidence reduction, suggesting that strengthening health system infrastructure is a key driver of progress toward the End TB targets.
Evidence: a 1-unit increase in the TB-specific service readiness index is associated with a 3.1% increase in TB incidence reduction ( β : 3.1; 95% CrI: 0.9, 6.1).

Indicators of the preparedness and readiness of health facilities such as readiness for chronic respiratory disease and TB were measured by using data from the EPHI Service Availability and Readiness Assessment survey [ 33 ].
17.Rationale: The Bayesian multivariable model reported in the passage shows a positive association between the TB-specific service readiness index and percentage reduction in TB incidence (3.1% increase in reduction per 1-unit increase in readiness, credible interval excludes zero). This supports the inference that districts with better TB service preparedness/resources tend to achieve greater incidence reductions. While the passage does not prove causality, the observed association justifies the epidemiological conclusion that strengthening health system readiness is an important driver of progress toward End TB targets.

17.Option: The proportion of individuals with good knowledge about TB is positively associated with TB incidence reduction, indicating that public education campaigns are the most effective intervention for achieving national TB control goals.
Evidence: a 1% increase in the proportion of individuals with good knowledge about TB is associated with a 4.3% increase in TB incidence reduction [ β : 4.3%; 95% credible interval (CrI): 1.6, 6.9].
17.Rationale: The passage clearly reports a positive association between population-level TB knowledge and TB incidence reduction (4.3% increase in reduction per 1% increase in knowledge). However, the claim that public education campaigns are the "most effective intervention" is not supported by the data presented. The study reports associations for knowledge and for service readiness, but it does not compare the relative effectiveness of interventions or establish causality or ranking of interventions. Therefore the first clause (positive association) is supported, but the stronger conclusion that education campaigns are the most effective intervention cannot be derived from the passage alone.

18.Option: The associations between loneliness and incident CVD risk were not modified by social isolation or gender, despite the hypothesized stronger effect in South Korea due to its collectivist culture.
Evidence: We hypothesized that loneliness would be associated with an increased risk of incident CVD in both countries. However, given the stronger interdependent culture in South Korea, we hypothesized that loneliness would be more strongly associated with CVD incidence in South Korea than in the USA.
Loneliness was associated with a higher risk of developing CVD in both HRS and KLoSA.
In the fully adjusted model, feeling lonely was associated with a 16% and 15% higher likelihood of developing CVD in KLoSA and HRS, respectively.

No significant multiplicative interaction between loneliness and social isolation was found in HRS ( P = 0.11 with categorical social isolation; P = 0.22 with continuous social isolation) or KLoSA ( P = 0.43 with categorical social isolation; P = 0.48 with continuous social isolation), nor was any significant additive interaction observed in HRS (RERI=−0.04, 95% CI −0.27 to 0.19) or KLoSA (RERI: 0.04, 95% CI −0.21 to 0.3).

No significant multiplicative interaction between loneliness and gender was found in HRS ( P = 0.30) or KLoSA ( P = 0.56), nor was any significant additive interaction observed in HRS (RERI = 0.08, 95% CI=−0.12 ∼ 0.29) or KLoSA (RERI: −0.15, 95% CI −0.35 ∼ 0.06).
18.Rationale: The passage explicitly states the authors hypothesized a stronger loneliness–CVD association in South Korea, yet reports that loneliness was associated with increased CVD risk in both cohorts and provides statistical tests showing no significant multiplicative or additive interactions with social isolation or with gender. Thus the conclusion that associations were not modified by social isolation or gender, despite the prior hypothesis about cultural differences, is directly supported by the reported results.

18.Option: The observed effect sizes in both HRS and KLoSA for loneliness in relation to CVD are comparable with those found in prior studies, suggesting that loneliness is a consistently significant risk factor across diverse populations.
Evidence: A systematic review of empirical studies examining the association between loneliness and CVD published through 2015 [ 11 ], identified only four longitudinal studies. Except for one study with a small sample size [ 12 ], loneliness was consistently associated with a higher risk of developing CVD, and these associations were generally evident even after controlling for conventional risk factors and numerous potential confounders, including sociodemographics, health conditions, and risk behaviors [ 13–15 ].

While the recent systematic review [ 20 ] included eight studies not examined in the aforementioned review [ 11 ], all studies that examined loneliness and CVD incidence were conducted in Western countries, limiting the generalizability of their findings [ 21 ].
Loneliness was associated with a higher risk of developing CVD in both HRS and KLoSA.
In the fully adjusted model, feeling lonely was associated with a 16% and 15% higher likelihood of developing CVD in KLoSA and HRS, respectively.
In the meta-analysis of HRS and KLoSA, the fully adjusted HR for loneliness was 1.14 (95% CI: 1.06–1.23).
18.Rationale: The passage documents prior studies that generally found loneliness associated with increased CVD risk and reports that this study also found statistically significant associations in both countries. However, the passage does not provide numerical effect sizes from prior studies for direct comparison, nor does it claim explicit comparability of effect magnitudes across all prior research. Therefore, while the data support that loneliness is a significant risk factor in these samples (including a non-Western sample), the specific claim that observed effect sizes are comparable with those found in prior studies is not directly supported by explicit comparative data in the passage and is not strictly derivable from the provided text.

18.Option: The lack of significant interaction between loneliness and social isolation suggests that loneliness and social isolation operate through independent biological pathways in the development of CVD.
Evidence: Social isolation was assessed using the Berkman-Syme Social Network Index [ 32 ] administered in HRS and KLoSA at the study baseline, using information from four domains: (i) marital status, (ii) contact with close friends and relatives, (iii) participation in group activities, and (iv) participation in religious activities.

No significant multiplicative interaction between loneliness and social isolation was found in HRS ( P = 0.11 with categorical social isolation; P = 0.22 with continuous social isolation) or KLoSA ( P = 0.43 with categorical social isolation; P = 0.48 with continuous social isolation), nor was any significant additive interaction observed in HRS (RERI=−0.04, 95% CI −0.27 to 0.19) or KLoSA (RERI: 0.04, 95% CI −0.21 to 0.3).

In both countries, those who were lonely also had lower Social Network Index scores, engaged in less physical activity, consumed less alcohol, were more likely to be women, to be less educated, and to have a higher prevalence of diabetes and hypertension ( Table 1 ).

In both samples, physical activity (14.3%, P = 0.03 in HRS; 1.3%, P = 0.04 in KLoSA) and alcohol consumption (3.9%, P < 0.001 in HRS; 1.3%, P < 0.001 in KLoSA) emerged as statistically significant mediators.
18.Rationale: The passage reports statistical tests showing no significant interaction between loneliness and social isolation, and describes measurement of social isolation and mediation analyses by health behaviors. We created a new category of tool to reflect this focus on consistency within a study.
47.Rationale: The passage indicates the framework's purpose is to classify evidence based on statistical significance and consistency across analytical methods. It does not state that the classification is intended to evaluate clinical implications or readiness for therapeutic application. Other parts of the passage mention only two tools that addressed clinical implications, but the Markozannes framework is presented specifically as an assessment of internal consistency of MR evidence, so inferring a primary focus on clinical/therapeutic implications is not supported by the text.

47.Option: The framework by Markozannes et al. provides a scoring system to quantify the overall methodological quality of Mendelian randomization studies, including risk of bias, reporting, and conduct.
Evidence: We identified a newly developed framework that focuses on evaluating the strength and consistency of MR findings: Markozannes et al. [ 13 ] proposed a structured decision flow that classifies each exposure–outcome association into one of four levels, which they call “robust evidence”, “probably”, “suggestive”, and “insufficient”.

Their classification depends on whether the main MR estimate reaches statistical significance and whether results from additional methods, such as MR-Egger, weighted median, MR-PRESSO, or multivariable MR, show consistent direction and significance.
We view this as an assessment of consistency rather than robustness; indeed others have reconceived the options as “consistent”, “concordant”, “inconsistent”, and “inadequate” [ 34 ].
We created a new category of tool to reflect this focus on consistency within a study.
47.Rationale: The passage describes Markozannes et al.'s output as a structured decision flow that classifies exposure–outcome associations into four descriptive levels based on significance and consistency across methods. It does not describe a numerical scoring system quantifying overall methodological quality, nor does it state that it assesses risk of bias, reporting, and conduct comprehensively. Thus interpreting the framework as a general methodological quality scoring tool is not supported by the provided text.

47.Option: The framework by Markozannes et al. classifies MR associations into levels of evidence based on consistency across multiple analytical methods, which may complement risk of bias tools by indicating whether a causal interpretation is supported consistently across analyses.
Evidence: We identified a newly developed framework that focuses on evaluating the strength and consistency of MR findings: Markozannes et al. [ 13 ] proposed a structured decision flow that classifies each exposure–outcome association into one of four levels, which they call “robust evidence”, “probably”, “suggestive”, and “insufficient”.

Their classification depends on whether the main MR estimate reaches statistical significance and whether results from additional methods, such as MR-Egger, weighted median, MR-PRESSO, or multivariable MR, show consistent direction and significance.
We view this as an assessment of consistency rather than robustness; indeed others have reconceived the options as “consistent”, “concordant”, “inconsistent”, and “inadequate” [ 34 ].
We created a new category of tool to reflect this focus on consistency within a study.
47.Rationale: The passage explicitly states that the Markozannes et al. framework is a structured decision flow that classifies exposure–outcome associations into evidence levels based on whether the primary MR estimate is statistically significant and whether additional MR methods yield consistent direction and significance. The authors characterize this as assessing 'consistency' and note they created a new tool category for this focus. Therefore the option accurately captures the primary function of the framework and reasonably notes that it complements (rather than replaces) risk-of-bias tools by indicating consistency of causal interpretations across analyses.

47.Option: The framework by Markozannes et al. is intended to replace existing risk of bias tools by providing a more rigorous and standardized method for evaluating the validity of causal inferences in Mendelian randomization studies.
Evidence: We identified a newly developed framework that focuses on evaluating the strength and consistency of MR findings: Markozannes et al. [ 13 ] proposed a structured decision flow that classifies each exposure–outcome association into one of four levels, which they call “robust evidence”, “probably”, “suggestive”, and “insufficient”.

Their classification depends on whether the main MR estimate reaches statistical significance and whether results from additional methods, such as MR-Egger, weighted median, MR-PRESSO, or multivariable MR, show consistent direction and significance.
We view this as an assessment of consistency rather than robustness; indeed others have reconceived the options as “consistent”, “concordant”, “inconsistent”, and “inadequate” [ 34 ].
We created a new category of tool to reflect this focus on consistency within a study.
47.Rationale: The passage presents the Markozannes framework as a new tool focused on assessing the consistency/strength of MR findings and states that the authors created a new category to reflect this focus. It does not claim that the framework is meant to replace existing risk-of-bias tools or that it provides a comprehensive standardized method for evaluating validity of causal inferences. Rather, it is framed as an additional, distinct category assessing consistency within studies. Thus the replacement claim is not supported by the passage.

48.Option: Greater vegetable diversity appears to lower T2D risk in males due to their higher susceptibility to oxidative stress and lower antioxidant capacity, which may be mitigated by a diet rich in antioxidant-containing vegetables.
Evidence: Three or more subtypes of vegetables reduced T2D incidence only in males by 15%–16% ( Table 4 ).
Both sex and adiposity can modify biological and socio-behavioral pathways linking dietary diversity to T2D, yet modifiers remain unexplored.
48.Rationale: The passage supports the empirical claim that greater vegetable diversity reduced T2D incidence only in males (first evidence quote). However, the specific mechanistic claim that this effect is "due to their higher susceptibility to oxidative stress and lower antioxidant capacity" is not stated or supported anywhere in the passage. The passage discusses that sex and adiposity can modify associations and offers possible biological pathways in general, but it does not provide evidence about males' oxidative stress or antioxidant capacity. Because the causal mechanism is not provided in the passage, the overall option cannot be fully derived from the study data and is therefore incorrect.

48.Option: Consuming five major food groups and four subtypes of vegetables was associated with lower T2D incidence across all subgroups, indicating that dietary diversity has a uniform protective effect regardless of sex or obesity status.
Evidence: For total dietary diversity and vegetable diversity, the greatest diversity level was associated with lower T2D incidence [0.86 (0.75, 0.98) and 0.90 (0.83, 0.98), respectively] compared with the lowest scores ( Table 3 ).
Three or more subtypes of vegetables reduced T2D incidence only in males by 15%–16% ( Table 4 ).
Associations were also modified by sex and obesity, although overall tests of group difference were nonsignificant.
Four and five major food groups reduced T2D incidence by 17% and 21% in those without central obesity
48.Rationale: Although the passage reports that higher total and vegetable diversity were associated with lower T2D incidence overall (first quote), the effects were not uniform across all subgroups. Vegetable diversity reductions occurred "only in males" (second quote), and reductions in major food groups were observed specifically in those without central obesity (fourth quote). The passage explicitly notes that associations were modified by sex and obesity (third quote). Therefore, the claim of a uniform protective effect across all subgroups is not supported by the presented data.

48.Option: The association between plant-protein diversity and T2D risk was stronger in individuals with central obesity, as indicated by the larger hazard ratios and narrower confidence intervals in this subgroup.
Evidence: Across countries, consuming four to five subtypes of plant-protein sources was associated with a lower incidence of T2D [HR 0.78 (95% CI 0.65, 0.93)] compared with no consumption ( Table 3 ).

Individuals both with and without obesity showed an inverse association between plant-protein diversity and incident T2D, but only participants without central obesity reporting five subtypes had an 18% lower incidence [0.82 (0.68, 1.00)] compared with no intake.
Associations were different between the groups with and without obesity ( P = 0.04).
48.Rationale: The passage reports inverse associations of plant-protein diversity overall and highlights benefit specifically among participants without central obesity (second quote). It does not report stronger associations in those with central obesity; in fact, the evidence points to benefit in the subgroup without central obesity. The statement that the association was stronger in individuals with central obesity is therefore contrary to the data presented and cannot be derived from the passage.

48.Option: Specific subpopulations, such as females and individuals without central obesity, may benefit most from greater overall and within-group dietary diversity for type 2 diabetes prevention.
Evidence: There was a consistent inverse association of plant-protein diversity with incident T2D in females and no clear pattern in males.
Females consuming three subtypes of plant protein had a 25% lower incidence of T2D [0.75 (0.62, 0.90)] compared with no consumption.

Individuals both with and without obesity showed an inverse association between plant-protein diversity and incident T2D, but only participants without central obesity reporting five subtypes had an 18% lower incidence [0.82 (0.68, 1.00)] compared with no intake.
Five food groups reduced T2D incidence in females [0.86 (0.77, 0.96)], with a similar pattern in males.
Four and five major food groups reduced T2D incidence by 17% and 21% in those without central obesity
48.Rationale: The passage provides multiple findings indicating that benefits of dietary diversity vary by subgroup: plant-protein diversity showed a consistent inverse association in females with a large effect size for three subtypes (first two quotes), and some of the strongest reductions in T2D incidence for total dietary diversity were observed in participants without central obesity (third and fifth quotes). The evidence supports the inference that specific subpopulations — notably females and individuals without central obesity — may derive disproportionate benefits from greater dietary diversity for T2D prevention.

49.Option: The lack of difference in counselling uptake between the two arms suggests that the digital screening tool did not improve the overall effectiveness of the health service in identifying and supporting vulnerable individuals.
Evidence: The cluster-level geometric mean prevalence of CMD, defined as an SSQ score of ≥8, was 19.4% when ACASI was used and 14.1% when using SAQ ( Table 2 ), and there was weak evidence of an association of CMD with the ACASI trial arm [risk ratio (RR) 1.37, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.99, 1.89; P = .056].

ACASI data collection was associated with increased reporting of all forms of IPV (cluster-level geometric mean prevalence 41.1% compared with 20.8%, RR 1.99, 95% CI 1.55, 2.57; P < .001) ( Table 2 ).

There was no evidence of a difference between arms in the proportion of all participants who received counselling [cluster-level geometric mean prevalence 13.2% vs 12.1%, adjusted risk ratio (aRR) 1.09, 95% CI 0.70–1.71; P = .71].
49.Rationale: The passage shows that ACASI increased detected prevalence of CMD (weak evidence) and substantially increased reporting of IPV, so it did improve identification of potential cases. However, counselling uptake did not differ between arms. The option asserts that the digital tool did not improve overall effectiveness in 'identifying and supporting' vulnerable individuals, which is inconsistent with the evidence for identification. Therefore the broad negative claim about both identification and support is not derivable: identification improved (higher positive screens), but linkage to counselling (support) did not increase.

49.Option: The administration of screening for common mental disorders and intimate partner violence using ACASI elicited more potential cases than did screening with paper questionnaires, but did not increase the number of participants who received counselling.
Evidence: The cluster-level geometric mean prevalence of CMD, defined as an SSQ score of ≥8, was 19.4% when ACASI was used and 14.1% when using SAQ ( Table 2 ), and there was weak evidence of an association of CMD with the ACASI trial arm [risk ratio (RR) 1.37, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.99, 1.89; P = .056].

ACASI data collection was associated with increased reporting of all forms of IPV (cluster-level geometric mean prevalence 41.1% compared with 20.8%, RR 1.99, 95% CI 1.55, 2.57; P < .001) ( Table 2 ).

There was no evidence of a difference between arms in the proportion of all participants who received counselling [cluster-level geometric mean prevalence 13.2% vs 12.1%, adjusted risk ratio (aRR) 1.09, 95% CI 0.70–1.71; P = .71].
49.Rationale: The passage explicitly reports higher prevalence of positive screens for CMD and markedly higher reporting of IPV with ACASI compared with SAQ, indicating ACASI elicited more potential cases. It also explicitly states there was no evidence of a difference between arms in the proportion of participants who received counselling. Thus both parts of the statement are directly supported by the passage.

49.Option: The observed increase in the prevalence of CMD and IPV when using ACASI could have been due to an increase in the false-positive rate rather than a decrease in the false-negative rate.
Evidence: ACASI data collection was associated with increased reporting of all forms of IPV (cluster-level geometric mean prevalence 41.1% compared with 20.8%, RR 1.99, 95% CI 1.55, 2.57; P < .001) ( Table 2 ).

The cluster-level geometric mean prevalence of CMD, defined as an SSQ score of ≥8, was 19.4% when ACASI was used and 14.1% when using SAQ ( Table 2 ), and there was weak evidence of an association of CMD with the ACASI trial arm [risk ratio (RR) 1.37, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.99, 1.89; P = .056].
Less evidence is available for the effectiveness of ACASI for other sensitive topics such as experience of abuse [ 4 ] or symptoms of mental health disorders, particularly in low-income settings.
49.Rationale: The passage documents higher prevalence with ACASI but provides no validation data (no gold-standard assessment) to determine whether the increased positives represent more true cases (reduced false-negatives) or more false-positives. The statement about false-positive versus false-negative rates is speculative and not supported by the presented data. The passage even notes limited evidence about ACASI's effectiveness for these topics in low-income settings, meaning one cannot infer the increase was specifically due to higher false-positive rates.

49.Option: The higher reporting of IPV in men using ACASI may reflect greater willingness among men to disclose abuse due to the perceived anonymity of the digital tool, which aligns with traditional masculine norms of emotional restraint.
Evidence: ACASI is thought to remove social pressure and give a sense of privacy [ 4 ].
ACASI was associated with increased prevalence of reports of all forms of IPV in both men and women ( Table 4 ) with no evidence of interaction by gender ( t = 0.15, P = 0.88).
In men using ACASI, 29.4% reported emotional violence, 8.4% physical, 4.5% severe physical, and 2.2% sexual IPV.
49.Rationale: While the passage supports that ACASI may reduce social pressure and was associated with increased reporting among men, it does not provide any data or discussion about cultural concepts such as 'traditional masculine norms of emotional restraint' or that men's higher reporting specifically reflects willingness due to anonymity. The causal explanation invoking masculine norms is external to the data and not derivable from the passage.

49.Option: The feasibility and acceptability of ACASI in low-income settings are well established, as demonstrated by high participant engagement and low technical failure rates during the trial.
Evidence: Less evidence is available for the effectiveness of ACASI for other sensitive topics such as experience of abuse [ 4 ] or symptoms of mental health disorders, particularly in low-income settings.
The trial enrolled from 20 February to 10 June 2022, encompassing 71 team workdays (clusters) and 1240 participants ( Supplementary Table S1 ).
In the ACASI arm, 673 participants were enrolled during 39 workdays, with a median 17 (range 5–29) recruited per day.
49.Rationale: The passage does not claim that feasibility and acceptability of ACASI in low-income settings are 'well established'; it explicitly states less evidence is available for effectiveness in such settings. While the trial successfully enrolled participants using ACASI, the passage provides no measures of 'high participant engagement' or any data on technical failure rates. Therefore the strong assertion that feasibility and acceptability are well established and demonstrated by low technical failures is not supported by the presented information.

50.Option: The validity of COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness studies conducted at the primary care level may be jeopardized if vaccination status influences self-testing behavior and self-test results influence GP consultation, particularly when these effects occur in opposite directions.
Evidence: COVID-19 vaccination status may impact self-testing behaviours, e.g. if vaccinated persons are more likely to self-test [ 11 ], and knowing the self-test result may affect GP consultation behaviour.
The combination of these two effects could introduce bias (see a numerical example in Supplementary Tables S1–S3 ).

In Fig. 2A, the non-causal path COVID-19 vaccination → self-testing → self-test result ← SARS-CoV-2 infection (in bold) is open because, by design, we restrict based on GP consultation, which is a descendant of the collider variable self-test result [ 19 ].
In all scenarios where the probability of GP consultation after a positive or negative self-test result (but not both) varied from 1, we observed a greater bias ...

More extreme bias occurred when the probability of GP consultation differed from 1 after both a positive and negative self-test. The most extreme bias of 45% occurred with a 20% VE, 30% self-testing among the unvaccinated and 2.5 times higher self-testing among the vaccinated, and the largest difference between GP consultation behaviours after a positive or negative self-test result...
50.Rationale: The passage explicitly states vaccination can affect self-testing and that knowing the self-test result can change GP consultation behavior. It describes how these linked effects open a non-causal path that can introduce bias in TND primary-care VE estimates, and the simulations show larger bias when consultation probabilities after positive vs negative self-tests differ (i.e. when effects operate in opposite directions). Therefore this inference is directly supported by the Passage Body.

50.Option: The primary care test-negative design is inherently invalid in settings where self-testing is prevalent, regardless of vaccination status or consultation behavior.
Evidence: This bias in COVID-19 VE can be mitigated by adjusting the logistic regression model by self-test use (yes/no), if this information is collected within the study without misclassification.
While a selection bias is introduced into the study, it can be mitigated with techniques used to adjust for confounding, such as regression modelling [ 20 , 21 ].
According to Fig. 1, there are no non-causal paths open between COVID-19 vaccination and SARS-CoV-2 infection. The causal odds ratio, and hereafter unbiased VE, may thus be estimated.
50.Rationale: The passage does not claim the TND is inherently invalid where self-testing is common. Instead, it demonstrates that bias can arise but also shows this bias can be mitigated (for example by adjusting for self-test use). Thus the stronger statement of inherent invalidity regardless of circumstances is not supported by the passage.

50.Option: The most extreme bias in vaccine effectiveness estimates occurs when vaccinated individuals are less likely to self-test and more likely to consult the GP after a negative result.
Evidence: The most extreme bias of 45% occurred with a 20% VE, 30% self-testing among the unvaccinated and 2.5 times higher self-testing among the vaccinated, and the largest difference between GP consultation behaviours after a positive or negative self-test result (i.e. consultation probability ratio of 2 after a positive self-test, combined with consultation probability ratio of 0.5 after a negative self-test, or vice versa) ( Supplementary Fig. S2 and Table S4 ).

In all scenarios where the probability of GP consultation after a positive or negative self-test result (but not both) varied from 1, we observed a greater bias with ... a greater effect of vaccination on self-testing ( −2% to 18% for a probability ratio of 2.5 versus −4% to 6% for an probability ratio of 1.5).
50.Rationale: The passage reports the most extreme bias occurring when vaccinated individuals were more likely (not less likely) to self-test (2.5 times higher). It does not identify the specific configuration stated in this option (vaccinated less likely to self-test and more likely to consult after a negative result) as producing the worst bias. Therefore this option is not supported by the passage.

50.Option: The use of self-tests in the general population may reduce the overall burden on primary care systems by decreasing unnecessary GP consultations for individuals who test negative.
Evidence: Thus, an individual with respiratory infection symptoms can know their COVID-19 status before deciding to see their general practitioner (GP).
Little is known about the proportion of people with respiratory infection symptoms who self-test.
This effect may occur through a person testing negative being more likely to consult the GP, or a person testing positive being more likely to consult the GP.
50.Rationale: While the passage notes that self-testing allows people to know their COVID-19 status before deciding to see a GP, it does not present evidence that self-testing reduces GP burden overall. In fact, the passage explicitly says knowledge of the result may either increase or decrease GP consultation (a person testing negative may be more likely to consult, or a person testing positive may be more likely to consult). The direction and net effect on primary care burden are therefore not determined in the Passage Body, so this inference cannot be derived.

50.Option: Self-testing behavior is primarily driven by healthcare-seeking behavior, which is already controlled for in test-negative design studies, minimizing the risk of bias.
Evidence: healthcare-seeking behaviour, defined as one’s propensity to seek care, is a determinant of vaccination, GP consultation, and self-testing [ 7 ].
In TND studies, it is generally assumed that healthcare-seeking behaviour is (at least partially) controlled for by design [ 7 ].
This study focuses on bias emerging from an effect of vaccination on self-testing that is independent from healthcare-seeking behaviour.
50.Rationale: The passage acknowledges that healthcare-seeking behaviour influences self-testing and is assumed to be (partially) controlled in the TND. However, the authors explicitly focus on bias arising from an effect of vaccination on self-testing that is independent of healthcare-seeking behaviour. Therefore self-testing is not described as being solely driven by healthcare-seeking behaviour nor is the risk of bias minimized simply by TND control of healthcare-seeking; bias can still occur. The option overstates and misrepresents the passage.

51.Option: The use of probabilistic trend categorization—such as stable, increase, or decrease—enhances the utility of forecasts for decision-making by providing interpretable, actionable insights into future epidemic trajectories.
Evidence: Lastly, the use of prediction samples allows us to assign probabilities to different interpretable trend categories (stable, increase, and decrease) by using thresholds agreed with disease and operations experts at all geographies.
This provides enough foresight to be useful, with meaningfully small uncertainty, agreed with end users of the forecasts.
When used well, numerical forecasts help to inform healthcare planning to allocate resources more effectively, improving health outcomes.
51.Rationale: The passage explicitly states that prediction samples are used to assign probabilities to interpretable trend categories (stable, increase, decrease) using thresholds agreed with experts. It also states the forecasts provide useful foresight agreed with end users and that numerical forecasts inform healthcare planning. From these statements, it is directly supported that probabilistic trend categorization produces interpretable, actionable insights that enhance forecast utility for decision-making.

51.Option: The probabilistic trend categorization enables modelers to identify and exclude underperforming models during weekly quality checks, improving forecast reliability.
Evidence: While quantitative scoring is a key component in developing our ensemble, within-team expert judgment is necessary to exclude models weekly.
Each week, models are first inspected by the team (applying expert judgment) and then candidate models are ensembled.

Lastly, the use of prediction samples allows us to assign probabilities to different interpretable trend categories (stable, increase, and decrease) by using thresholds agreed with disease and operations experts at all geographies.
51.Rationale: The passage describes two separate processes: (a) weekly model inspection and exclusion driven by quantitative scoring and within-team expert judgment, and (b) the use of prediction samples to assign probabilities to interpretable trend categories. The text does not state that the probabilistic trend categorization is the tool used to identify or exclude underperforming models. Therefore the specific causal claim that trend categorization enables model exclusion during weekly quality checks is not supported by the passage.

51.Option: The use of a 14-day forecast horizon provides sufficient foresight for stakeholders to plan long-term healthcare infrastructure investments and staffing strategies.
Evidence: As a trade-off between long forecast horizons with high uncertainty and short horizons with lower utility, we chose a consistent 14-day horizon across all models. This provides enough foresight to be useful, with meaningfully small uncertainty, agreed with end users of the forecasts.

Public health and healthcare leaders better use scarce resources when they can predict hospital admissions and bed occupancy, reallocating staff and beds to elective care as emergency admissions decline.
51.Rationale: The passage states the 14-day horizon was chosen as a balance that 'provides enough foresight to be useful' for operational planning and reallocating resources. However, it does not claim or provide evidence that a 14-day horizon is sufficient for long-term infrastructure investment decisions or long-term staffing strategies, which typically require longer-term forecasts and planning horizons. Thus the option overstates the supported application of the 14-day horizon.

51.Option: The integration of mechanistic assumptions, such as susceptible depletion, could improve predictive performance at epidemic turning points, particularly for seasonally driven diseases like influenza and RSV.
Evidence: Our modeling suite focuses on statistical forecasts, following evidence of their strong performance in short-term forecasting tasks relative to strictly mechanistic approaches.

the primary model class used was a generalized additive model (GAM), which uses the semi-mechanistic assumption of a recent growth rate extrapolated forward in time [ 27 ] via the mgcv and gratia packages [ 28 , 29 ].
The COVID-19 forecasts have variation in their accuracy, with forecasts generally struggling in growth/decline phases, when the models are slow to adapt to changing trends ( Figure 4 ).
The COVID-19 Weighted Interval Score are more consistent over time than the influenza and RSV metrics, which score poorly near the peak.
51.Rationale: The passage documents that the team predominantly used statistical models (with a GAM that is semi-mechanistic) because of their short-term performance advantages over strictly mechanistic approaches. It also notes the models struggled during growth/decline phases and near peaks. However, the passage does not provide evidence that adding specific mechanistic assumptions (e.g., susceptible depletion) would improve performance at turning points; indeed it emphasizes preference for statistical approaches. The claim that integrating such mechanistic assumptions 'could improve' performance is speculative and not directly derivable from the passage.

52.Option: The higher incidence of medication abortions in outer regional, remote, and very remote areas compared to major cities indicates that women in these regions are more likely to prefer medication abortion over surgical abortion.
Evidence: The incidence rate of medication abortions relative to the incidence rate of surgical abortions (i.e. the ratio of medication abortions to surgical abortions) was higher in inner regional and outer regional/remote/very remote areas compared with major cities ( Fig. 3 ).

In 2020, the incidence rates of medication and surgical abortions in major cities were 5 per 1000 women and 8 per 1000 women, respectively. Conversely, in outer regional, remote, and very remote areas, the incidence rate of medication abortions (9 per 1000 women) in 2020 was three times that of surgical abortions (3 per 1000 women).

Surgical abortion care is limited outside metropolitan cities and there are areas in Australia that are regarded as “abortion deserts” where neither medication nor surgical abortion is available [ 4 , 22 ].
Previous research has shown that most women prefer one abortion method over another [ 19 ] and that abortion experiences are generally better when women receive the method of their choice [ 20 ].
52.Rationale: While the passage documents a higher incidence of medication abortions in nonmetropolitan areas and notes that most women have method preferences, it does not provide direct evidence that the observed geographic pattern is driven by women's preferences in those regions. The passage also states that surgical abortion care is limited outside metropolitan cities and that geographic/financial barriers may restrict choice, indicating availability likely influences observed incidence. Therefore, inferring that women in these regions are more likely to prefer medication abortion cannot be derived solely from the presented data.

52.Option: The higher incidence of medication abortions in nonmetropolitan areas is primarily due to the greater availability of telehealth services for medication abortion in those regions.
Evidence: The incidence rate of medication abortions relative to the incidence rate of surgical abortions (i.e. the ratio of medication abortions to surgical abortions) was higher in inner regional and outer regional/remote/very remote areas compared with major cities ( Fig. 3 ).

In 2020, the incidence rates of medication and surgical abortions in major cities were 5 per 1000 women and 8 per 1000 women, respectively. Conversely, in outer regional, remote, and very remote areas, the incidence rate of medication abortions (9 per 1000 women) in 2020 was three times that of surgical abortions (3 per 1000 women).
In 2015, the introduction of telehealth services for medication abortion facilitated expanded access in Australia, with the greatest benefit to rural and remote communities [ 24 ].
52.Rationale: The passage reports both higher medication abortion incidence in nonmetropolitan areas and that telehealth services facilitated expanded access benefiting rural and remote communities. However, it does not provide evidence that telehealth availability is the primary cause of the higher incidence. The data do not quantify the contribution of telehealth versus other factors (e.g. limited surgical services, cost, policy changes, PBS listing). Thus, the causal claim that telehealth is the primary reason is not supported by the passage alone.

52.Option: The strong geographical disparities in the abortion method used suggest that, for those who live in nonmetropolitan areas, there may be less opportunity to choose surgical abortion due to the limited availability of services.
Evidence: The incidence rate of medication abortions relative to the incidence rate of surgical abortions (i.e. the ratio of medication abortions to surgical abortions) was higher in inner regional and outer regional/remote/very remote areas compared with major cities ( Fig. 3 ).

In 2020, the incidence rates of medication and surgical abortions in major cities were 5 per 1000 women and 8 per 1000 women, respectively. Conversely, in outer regional, remote, and very remote areas, the incidence rate of medication abortions (9 per 1000 women) in 2020 was three times that of surgical abortions (3 per 1000 women).

Surgical abortion care is limited outside metropolitan cities and there are areas in Australia that are regarded as “abortion deserts” where neither medication nor surgical abortion is available [ 4 , 22 ].

Women who lived in outer regional/remote/very remote areas had increased odds of a medication abortion [adjusted odds ratio (AOR) 3.51 (95% CI 2.15, 5.74)] compared with women who lived in major cities.
52.Rationale: The passage documents clear geographic disparities (higher medication:surgical ratio in nonmetropolitan areas), quantifies increased odds of medication abortion for women in outer regional/remote areas, and explicitly states that surgical abortion care is limited outside metropolitan cities and that some areas are “abortion deserts.” Together, these statements support the epidemiological inference that limited availability of surgical services in nonmetropolitan areas likely reduces opportunity to choose surgical abortion and contributes to the observed method distribution.

52.Option: The increasing use of medication abortion over time reflects a growing national preference for non-surgical methods among young Australian women.
Evidence: Nationally, in our sample of women who were born in 1989–95, aged 18–24 years in 2012/13, the incidence of medication abortions increased over time whereas the incidence of surgical abortions decreased over time ( Fig. 1 ).

The surgical abortion rate decreased from 14 abortions per 1000 women aged 18–24 years in 2013 (95% CI 10, 14) ( Table 1 ) to 8 abortions per 1000 women aged 25–31 years in 2020 (95% CI 7, 10). Conversely, the incidence rate of medication abortions per 1000 women increased from 1 abortion per 1000 women aged 19–25 years in 2014 (95% CI 1, 2)—the year after mifepristone was listed on the PBS—to 6 abortions per 1000 women aged 25–31 years in 2020 (95% CI 5, 8).

Limited access to mifepristone for medication abortion has been available in Australia since 2006 through the Therapeutic Goods Administration Authorised Prescriber Scheme [ 23 ]. Wider availability only came about in 2013 once the combination regimen for early medication abortion was added to the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS), which is a list of medicines that are provided at a government-subsidized price [ 18 ].
Previous research has shown that most women prefer one abortion method over another [ 19 ] and that abortion experiences are generally better when women receive the method of their choice [ 20 ].
52.Rationale: Although the passage documents an increasing use of medication abortion over time, it also describes policy and access changes (PBS listing in 2013, telehealth introduction in 2015) that plausibly contributed to increased availability and use. The passage does not provide direct evidence that the temporal increase reflects a growing national preference among young women; preference data are mentioned in general but not shown to have changed over time or to drive the observed trend. Therefore, attributing the trend primarily to changing preferences is not supported by the presented data.

52.Option: The limited availability of surgical abortion in remote areas is due to higher rates of medical contraindications to medication abortion among women in those regions.
Evidence: Surgical abortion care is limited outside metropolitan cities and there are areas in Australia that are regarded as “abortion deserts” where neither medication nor surgical abortion is available [ 4 , 22 ].

The incidence rate of medication abortions relative to the incidence rate of surgical abortions (i.e. the ratio of medication abortions to surgical abortions) was higher in inner regional and outer regional/remote/very remote areas compared with major cities ( Fig. 3 ).
52.Rationale: The passage states that surgical abortion care is limited outside metropolitan cities and documents geographic differences in method incidence, but it provides no information about rates of medical contraindications to medication abortion by region. There is no evidence presented that contraindications are more common in remote areas or that they explain limited surgical availability. Thus, this causal attribution is unsupported by the passage.

54.Option: The increase in hospital discharge and event rates for stroke in Switzerland between 2004 and 2017 is primarily due to a rise in non-traditional cardiovascular risk factors such as sleep disorders and obesity, which have directly contributed to higher stroke incidence.
Evidence: The overall increase in hypertension, obesity, hypercholesterolemia, and sleep disorders in Switzerland between 2007 and 2017 could have a direct impact on stroke incidence [ 6 ].
Since 2004, life circumstances and stroke treatments have transformed in Switzerland and worldwide.

59.Rationale: Although prior studies (largely in high-income settings) have found inverse associations between greenness and overweight, the study's results across Latin American cities are mixed—null in Chile, slightly positive in Argentina (women), and negative in Mexico and Colombia—so a universal inverse association is not supported by the presented data.

59.Option: Neighbourhood characteristics in Latin America appear to influence BMI differently from those in the Global North, reinforcing the need for the generation of further evidence on residential associations in these settings.
Evidence: Most studies on neighbourhood features and BMI have been conducted in high-income countries in the Global North and it is unclear whether these patterns of associations are also observed in other regions of the world.

For intersection density (Models 2b and 3), associations with BMI were null among men and women in all countries.

There are inverse associations between neighbourhood education and BMI in Argentina and Chile for both men and women... In contrast, among men living in Colombia and Mexico, we observe a pattern in the opposite direction...

For neighbourhood greenness, after adjusting for individual education (Model 2c), associations with BMI among men and women were null in Chile, slightly positive in Argentina..., and negative in Mexico... and Colombia (although weaker).
59.Rationale: The authors explicitly note uncertainty about whether Global North patterns apply in other regions and hypothesized differences. The empirical findings show heterogeneous and sometimes contrasting associations (null, inverse, or positive) across countries and sexes for the same neighbourhood features, which is inconsistent with a single uniform pattern reported in high-income countries. This supports the inference that neighbourhood influences on BMI differ in Latin America and that more context-specific evidence is warranted.

61.Option: The method reduces bias from horizontal pleiotropy by using genetic instruments that are unlikely to exhibit indirect genetic effects, thereby improving the validity of causal estimates.
Evidence: This can be mitigated by selecting genetic instruments that are unlikely to exhibit indirect genetic effects.
